walkthroughs.body_html: SA Chief Ernst Rohm demanded a 'second revolution' and integration of the Reichswehr into the SA. The army insisted on its monopoly of arms. On 30 June 1934 SS units arrested and shot Rohm and around 85 victims including Strasser and Schleicher. The army's gratitude was sealed by the Fuhrer Oath on 2 August after Hindenburg's death, when Hitler combined the offices of President and Chancellor.

Ian Kershaw's concept of 'working towards the Fuhrer' explains how subordinates anticipated Hitler's wishes without explicit orders. The state apparatus competed: party, ministries, SS, Four Year Plan office (Goring) and military overlapped. Functionalist historians like Hans Mommsen argued this polycratic dynamic produced radicalisation through cumulative initiatives rather than master plans.

The Gestapo had only 7,000 officers in 1939 but relied on informers; Robert Gellately stressed widespread denunciation. Concentration camps under Eicke's Dachau model expanded after 1934. The 1935 Reich Citizenship Law and Nazi welfare programmes (Strength Through Joy, Winter Help) blended coercion and reward. Goebbels's Ministry of Propaganda coordinated media to manufacture consent.

mcqs.q: How did Hitler come to power in 1933?
options: Hitler won an outright majority in the 1932 presidential election.
He was legally appointed Chancellor by President Hindenburg as part of a conservative political deal, after the Nazis became the largest party in the Reichstag.
It was a battle in which the SA tried to overthrow Hitler.
Hitler seized power through a violent coup or revolution.

mcqs.q: Why did Hitler order the Night of the Long Knives in 1934?
options: Goebbels invented television specifically to broadcast Nazi propaganda.
To eliminate Ernst Röhm and the SA leadership, reassure the army of his authority, and remove rivals — securing the army's loyalty when Hindenburg died weeks later.
Hitler purged the SA because they were Communists.
It was a battle in which the SA tried to overthrow Hitler.

mcqs.q: How effective was Nazi propaganda in winning popular support?
options: It was a battle in which the SA tried to overthrow Hitler.
Nazi propaganda was so powerful that Germans believed whatever Hitler said.
Most effective where it reinforced existing views (anti-Versailles, fear of communism, national pride); less so when contradicting daily experience or established religious belief.
Goebbels invented television specifically to broadcast Nazi propaganda.
